concerns.text: The plan states that the regression will “fit a linear regression (or GAM) … to model a systematic correction term” (Summary, line 1‑2). This implies a causal interpretation of the relationship between density features and the residuals, but the design is purely correlational. The claim of a “systematic correction term” is not justified without a causal framework.

Time‑Series 10‑fold CV is used, yet the plan treats each integer n as an independent observation. Autocorrelation in the sequential data reduces the effective sample size, which is not accounted for in power calculations or significance testing.

The regression includes only prime‑density predictors (π(n), 1/ln n, Σ 1/p) and omits any term for the underlying trend in n itself. Without controlling for the deterministic growth of the residuals with n, omitted‑variable bias may confound the estimated effects of the density features.

The feature Σ_{p≤n} 1/p is introduced as a “cumulative prime density weighted by partition weight” but its theoretical justification as a proxy for prime density is not provided, raising concerns about construct validity of this predictor.
The schema defines the field `inv_ln_n` (line 12) but the data model and plan consistently use the name `inv_log_n`. This naming mismatch will cause schema validation failures for `features.csv`.

The `model_output.schema.yaml` requires fields `model_type`, `R2_cv`, `null_model_R2`, and `null_model_MSE` which are not produced or documented in the plan's `model_results.json` description. The plan only mentions `coefficients`, `intercept`, `r_squared`, `p_values`, `fdr_corrected_p_values`, and `mse_cv`.
The `regression_output.schema.yaml` expects fields `mse` and `cv_mse`, but the plan's output (`model_results.json`) provides only `mse_cv`. This discrepancy will cause the contract tests to fail.

The validation target R(n)=log(p_P(n))−log(Q_as(n)) is defined using the asymptotic baseline Q_as(n), which itself is a function of the prime‑density quantities (π(n), 1/ln n, ∑_{p≤n}1/p) that are later used as predictors in the regression. This creates a circular/tautological validation: any correlation between R and those predictors is at least partially forced by the way Q_as was constructed, so the analysis cannot cleanly separate a genuine systematic correction from artefacts of the baseline definition.

The asymptotic expression Q_as(n) is used with a fixed constant C (derived from Meinardus’ theorem) that is not estimated from the data. Because C is not calibrated, systematic bias will inevitably appear in R(n) and may be (mis)attributed to the density predictors, making the claimed ‘significant correlation’ a trivial consequence of an un‑fitted baseline rather than an empirical discovery.

Linear (or GAM) regression on the log‑residuals assumes independent, homoskedastic errors. The residual series R(n) is generated from a sequential combinatorial process and is likely autocorrelated beyond what Newey‑West HAC adjustments can fully correct. A time‑series modelling framework (e.g., ARIMA or state‑space models) would be more appropriate for assessing predictive power of the density features.

The 10‑fold time‑series cross‑validation splits the ordered n‑range into contiguous blocks, but the evaluation metric (mean MSE) is compared to an intercept‑only null model using a paired t‑test that assumes independent fold errors. Because folds are temporally adjacent, their errors are not independent, violating the t‑test assumptions and potentially inflating significance.
The `regression_output.schema.yaml` expects fields `mse` and `cv_mse`, but the plan's output (`model_results.json`) provides only `mse_cv`. This discrepancy will cause the contract tests to fail.

new_concerns.location: plan.md:research.md §4.2/§4.3 "Calibrated Asymptotic Baseline" / "Residual & Feature Engineering"; plan.md T003/T005
new_concerns.text: The revision removes circularity only in the calibration CONSTANT C, not in the functional form of Q_as(n). Q_as(n)=C n^{-3/4} exp(2√(n/(2 ln n))) embeds 1/ln n in its exponent, so R(n)=log p_P(n)−log Q_as(n) contains the deterministic term −2√(n/2)·(1/ln n)^{1/2}. Regressing R(n) on the predictor 1/ln n (and π(n), ∑1/p, which are all smooth monotone functions of n and hence of 1/ln n) is therefore still partially tautological: a significant coefficient on 1/ln n is guaranteed by the baseline's construction, not evidence of a density-dependent correction. The linear control covariate n cannot absorb this nonlinear dependence. To break the circularity the plan must either (a) use a baseline whose functional form is free of the tested predictors (e.g., calibrate a flexible form on a disjoint training window and evaluate on held-out n, with the density predictors never entering Q_as), or (b) reframe the hypothesis so the target is prediction of R(n) beyond what the known analytic form of the residual already implies (e.g., test whether density features add predictive power over the closed-form residual skeleton −(3/4)ln n + 2√(n/(2 ln n)) as a baseline model).
